# <em>EDA in R</em> {#sec-eda-basic}

The `eda-basic.qmd` file includes some standard data pipeline functions for exploratory data analysis.

I've also included the code from the `eda-basic.qmd` file in the sections below. 

## Load data 

```{r}
#| label: eda-basic-qmd-pkgs
#| message: false
library(palmerpenguins)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

df <- palmerpenguins::penguins
```

## Manipulate and summarize 

```{r}
#| label: eda-basic-qmd-wrangle
#| warning: false 
#| message: false
df %>%
  dplyr::group_by(species, sex) %>%
  dplyr::summarise(
    dplyr::across(
      dplyr::where(is.numeric), 
      \(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)
      )
    ) %>%
  knitr::kable()
```

## Visualize 

```{r}
#| label: eda-basic-qmd-viz
#| warning: false 
#| message: false
df %>%
  ggplot2::ggplot(
    ggplot2::aes(
      x = bill_length_mm, 
      y = body_mass_g, 
      color = species)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point() + 
  ggplot2::geom_smooth(method = "lm")
```

## Recap

1. The `eda-basic.qmd` file loads `palmerpenguins::penguins`, groups the data by `species` and `sex`, and uses `dplyr::across()` with `where(is.numeric)` to compute the mean of every numeric column.

2. The scatter plot of `bill_length_mm` against `body_mass_g` adds a `geom_smooth(method = "lm")` line for each species. That linear relationship is what the model in [Modeling in Python](model-basic-py.qmd) estimates: body mass increases with bill length, and species shifts the baseline.

Next, [Lab 2: Project Architecture](lab02.qmd) loads the penguins data into `duckdb` and turns the model into a `vetiver` API.
